# A Multiphilic Descriptor for Chemical Reactivity

## Introduction and Theoretical Foundation

A novel multiphilic descriptor is proposed based on the integration of two established theoretical frameworks: Chattaraj's local philicity concept and Toro-Labbé's dual descriptor. By combining these complementary approaches, this new descriptor offers an enhanced tool for characterizing and predicting chemical reactivity at specific atomic sites within molecules.

## Definition of the Descriptor

The multiphilic descriptor is mathematically defined as the difference between the nucleophilic (W<sub>k</sub><sup>+</sup>) and electrophilic (W<sub>k</sub><sup>−</sup>) condensed philicity functions. This formulation captures the dual nature of chemical reactivity in a single, unified quantity, allowing for a more comprehensive assessment of how atomic sites behave during chemical interactions.

## Key Advantages

One of the principal strengths of this descriptor lies in its ability to simultaneously explain both the nucleophilicity and electrophilicity of atomic sites within a molecule. Rather than treating these two properties in isolation, the multiphilic descriptor provides an integrated perspective, enabling researchers to identify which sites are prone to nucleophilic behavior and which are more likely to act as electrophilic centers—all within a single analytical framework.

## Validation and Testing

The predictive capability of the descriptor was successfully evaluated across a range of selected molecular systems and chemical reactions. To further substantiate its reliability, force profiles were analyzed in representative cases, offering additional insight into the reaction mechanisms and confirming the descriptor's utility in capturing the underlying reactivity trends.

## Extension to Nucleophilicity Excess

Building upon this foundation, a related descriptor termed the nucleophilicity excess (ΔW<sup>−+</sup>) was defined and applied specifically to all-metal aromatic compounds. This extension allowed for the systematic study of both intramolecular and intermolecular reactivities, demonstrating the broader applicability of the approach to unconventional and challenging chemical systems.

## Conclusion

Together, these descriptors represent a valuable advancement in the field of conceptual density functional theory, providing chemists with robust and versatile tools for predicting and rationalizing site-specific reactivity across diverse chemical contexts.

# A Multiphilic Descriptor for Characterizing Atomic Reactivity

## Introduction and Theoretical Foundation

The prediction and rationalization of chemical reactivity remains a central goal in theoretical and computational chemistry. Conceptual density functional theory (DFT) has provided a rich set of reactivity descriptors that allow chemists to understand and anticipate how molecules will behave in chemical transformations. Among these, the concept of local philicity has proven particularly powerful, as it enables the characterization of site-specific reactivity within a molecule rather than treating reactivity as a global molecular property.

Building upon the established framework of local philicity and the more recently developed dual descriptor approaches, this work introduces a **multiphilic descriptor** designed to capture the ambiphilic nature of atomic sites. The descriptor is formally defined as the difference between the nucleophilic and electrophilic condensed philicity functions. By combining these two complementary aspects into a single quantity, the multiphilic descriptor is able to simultaneously characterize both the nucleophilicity and the electrophilicity of individual atomic sites within a molecule. This dual capability allows a given atom to be classified according to its preferential behavior—whether it is more prone to donate electron density (acting as a nucleophile) or to accept it (acting as an electrophile).

## Validation and Results

To assess the practical utility of the proposed descriptor, it was tested on a carefully selected set of molecular systems and chemical reactions. These test cases were chosen to span a range of reactivity scenarios, enabling a robust evaluation of the descriptor's predictive performance. The results demonstrated that the multiphilic descriptor successfully predicts the correct reactive behavior of atomic sites, correctly identifying the electrophilic and nucleophilic centers involved in the reactions under study. This confirms that the descriptor provides a reliable and physically meaningful measure of intramolecular reactivity.

In addition to the primary multiphilic descriptor, a closely related **nucleophilicity excess descriptor** was developed and examined. This descriptor was specifically validated on all-metal aromatic compounds, a challenging and unconventional class of systems whose electronic structures and reactivity patterns are often difficult to rationalize using traditional chemical intuition. The successful application of the nucleophilicity excess descriptor to these species underscores the generality and versatility of the approach.

## Conclusions

Taken together, the multiphilic and nucleophilicity excess descriptors offer a valuable and complementary set of tools for analyzing both intramolecular and intermolecular reactivities. By providing a unified means of characterizing the dual nucleophilic and electrophilic character of atomic sites, these descriptors extend the predictive power of conceptual DFT and open new avenues for the rational analysis of chemical reactivity across diverse molecular systems.

# Abstract

**A Unified Multiphilic Descriptor for Predicting Site-Selective Reactivity within the Framework of Conceptual Density Functional Theory**

Conceptual Density Functional Theory (CDFT) has established a robust hierarchy of reactivity descriptors—including electronegativity, chemical hardness, and the electrophilicity index—that quantify the intrinsic and site-specific reactive propensities of molecular systems. However, existing local descriptors often treat electrophilic and nucleophilic tendencies separately, limiting their predictive power for systems governed by ambiphilic behavior or competing reaction pathways. Here, we introduce a new **multiphilic descriptor (Δω<sub>k</sub><sup>±</sup>)** that unifies the electrophilic and nucleophilic character of individual atomic sites into a single, continuously varying quantity. The proposed descriptor is constructed from the dual-descriptor formalism combined with the global electrophilicity index, thereby simultaneously encoding charge-transfer capacity, local polarizability, and the direction of preferred electron flow. We formalize its mathematical foundation using a finite-difference approximation of the Fukui functions and derive its variational behavior under external perturbation. The descriptor was benchmarked against a diverse set of organic and organometallic systems, including Michael acceptors, 1,3-dipolar cycloaddition partners, and ambident nucleophiles, using range-separated hybrid functionals. Our results demonstrate that Δω<sub>k</sub><sup>±</sup> correctly predicts site selectivity and relative reactivity orderings in agreement with experimental regiochemical outcomes and high-level computational reference data, outperforming conventional single-mode local indices in cases of ambiphilic reactivity. Furthermore, we show that the descriptor provides mechanistic insight into the interplay between charge- and orbital-controlled interactions, offering a practical tool for the rational design of reactive intermediates and catalysts. These findings extend the CDFT toolkit and establish a transferable framework for anticipating chemical reactivity across broad classes of molecular transformations.

---

# The Multiphilic Descriptor in Conceptual DFT

## Key Idea

The multiphilic descriptor is a reactivity index developed within **conceptual density functional theory (CDFT)** to simultaneously characterize both the **electrophilic and nucleophilic** capabilities of a molecule at specific atomic sites. It addresses a limitation of earlier local reactivity descriptors by combining information about a site's tendency to accept electrons (electrophilicity) with its tendency to donate electrons (nucleophilicity) into a single, unified index.

## Definition

The multiphilic descriptor, denoted **Δω_k**, is defined as the **difference between the electrophilic and nucleophilic condensed philicity functions**:

$$\Delta\omega_k = \omega_k^{+} - \omega_k^{-}$$

where:

- $\omega_k^{+} = \omega \, f_k^{+}$ is the local electrophilicity (using the Fukui function for nucleophilic attack, $f_k^+$)
- $\omega_k^{-} = \omega \, f_k^{-}$ is the local nucleophilicity (using the Fukui function for electrophilic attack, $f_k^-$)
- $\omega$ is the **global electrophilicity index**, defined as $\omega = \mu^2 / 2\eta$ (with $\mu$ the chemical potential and $\eta$ the chemical hardness)

This can equivalently be written as:

$$\Delta\omega_k = \omega\,(f_k^{+} - f_k^{-}) = \omega\,\Delta f_k$$

where $\Delta f_k$ is the **dual descriptor**.

## Interpretation

- A **positive value** ($\Delta\omega_k > 0$) indicates that the site is favored toward **electrophilic** behavior (electron-accepting, susceptible to nucleophilic attack).
- A **negative value** ($\Delta\omega_k < 0$) indicates that the site is favored toward **nucleophilic** behavior (electron-donating, susceptible to electrophilic attack).

The descriptor thus provides an effective tool for predicting the most favorable sites for both types of reactions from a single quantity.

## Relevant References

The multiphilic descriptor is most directly associated with:

- **Padmanabhan, J.; Parthasarathi, R.; Elango, M.; Subramanian, V.; Krishnamoorthy, B. S.; Gutierrez-Oliva, S.; Toro-Labbé, A.; Roy, D. R.; Chattaraj, P. K.** "Multiphilic Descriptor for Chemical Reactivity and Selectivity." *Journal of Physical Chemistry A*, **2007**, *111*(37), 9130–9138.

Foundational concepts it builds upon include:

- **Parr, R. G.; Szentpály, L. v.; Liu, S.** "Electrophilicity Index." *Journal of the American Chemical Society*, **1999**, *121*, 1922 — for the global electrophilicity index.

- **Chattaraj, P. K.; Maiti, B.; Sarkar, U.** "Philicity: A Unified Treatment of Chemical Reactivity and Selectivity." *Journal of Physical Chemistry A*, **2003**, *107*, 4973 — for the local philicity concept.

- **Morell, C.; Grand, A.; Toro-Labbé, A.** "New Dual Descriptor for Chemical Reactivity." *Journal of Physical Chemistry A*, **2005**, *109*, 205 — for the dual descriptor, which forms the basis of the multiphilic index.

---

*Note: If you require the exact page numbers or wording for a formal citation, I recommend verifying these details against the original publications, as I may not reproduce every bibliographic detail with perfect accuracy.*

# Abstract

**A Dual Descriptor for Predicting Nucleophilic and Electrophilic Sites: Application to All-Metal Aromatic Compounds**

The identification of reactive sites toward electrophilic and nucleophilic attack remains a central challenge in the rational design of chemical reactivity. Here we present a dual descriptor derived from conceptual density functional theory (DFT) that simultaneously characterizes the propensity of a molecular site to undergo either nucleophilic or electrophilic attack. Defined as the difference between the nucleophilic and electrophilic Fukui functions, Δf(**r**) = f⁺(**r**) − f⁻(**r**), the dual descriptor yields a single, sign-dependent field: regions where Δf(**r**) > 0 correspond to sites favorable for nucleophilic attack (electrophilic centers), while regions where Δf(**r**) < 0 indicate sites favorable for electrophilic attack (nucleophilic centers). This unified formulation overcomes the ambiguity of interpreting the two Fukui functions separately and provides a robust, orbital-based criterion for site selectivity that is fully consistent with the principle of hard and soft acids and bases.

We apply the dual descriptor to a series of all-metal aromatic clusters, including Al₄²⁻ and related main-group and transition-metal systems whose delocalized σ- and π-electron frameworks confer aromatic stability. Analysis of the condensed and molecular dual-descriptor fields reveals a well-defined alternation of electrophilic and nucleophilic regions distributed around the cluster periphery, in agreement with the multiple-fold aromaticity and symmetry of these species. The predicted reactive sites correlate with computed interaction energies and geometries for model attacks by representative electrophiles and nucleophiles, validating the descriptor's predictive capacity in these unconventional bonding environments.

Our results demonstrate that the dual descriptor is a transferable and computationally efficient tool for anticipating regioselectivity, extending its utility from organic and coordination chemistry to the emerging class of all-metal aromatic compounds. These findings offer new insight into the reactivity patterns governed by metal-based aromaticity and provide a predictive framework for the targeted functionalization of metallic clusters.

counterfactuals.output:
# Multiphilic Descriptors: Dual Reactivity Characterization

## Conceptual Foundation

The **multiphilic descriptor** (often denoted Δf(**r**)) emerges from conceptual Density Functional Theory (DFT) as a tool to simultaneously assess both electrophilic and nucleophilic tendencies at atomic sites. It is defined as the difference between the two Fukui functions:

$$\Delta f(\mathbf{r}) = f^+(\mathbf{r}) - f^-(\mathbf{r})$$

where:
- **f⁺(r)** measures susceptibility toward **nucleophilic attack** (site's electrophilicity)
- **f⁻(r)** measures susceptibility toward **electrophilic attack** (site's nucleophilicity)

## How It Captures Both Behaviors Simultaneously

The elegance lies in the **sign and magnitude** of the single quantity:

| Condition | Interpretation |
|-----------|----------------|
| **Δf(r) > 0** | Site is predominantly **electrophilic** (favors nucleophilic attack) |
| **Δf(r) < 0** | Site is predominantly **nucleophilic** (favors electrophilic attack) |

Because both Fukui functions are combined into one expression, a **single scan** reveals the *net electronic disposition* of every atom. A large positive value flags strong electron-accepting centers; a large negative value flags strong electron-donating centers. This avoids examining two separate maps and directly ranks the **dual philicity** of competing sites.

### Enhanced Version: Multiphilic Descriptor with Global Weighting

Often the local descriptor is scaled by the **global electrophilicity index (ω)**:

$$\Delta\omega(\mathbf{r}) = \omega \cdot \Delta f(\mathbf{r})$$

This incorporates the molecule's overall electron-accepting power, improving intermolecular comparisons.

## Computing the Descriptor

Using a **finite difference approximation** with condensed (atom-centered) values via population analysis:

$$f_k^+ = q_k(N) - q_k(N+1)$$
$$f_k^- = q_k(N-1) - q_k(N)$$

where q_k is the electronic population on atom *k* for systems with N, N+1, and N−1 electrons. Three single-point calculations (neutral, anion, cation) suffice.

## Testing Along Reaction Paths

The descriptor becomes especially powerful when evaluated as a **function of the reaction coordinate**, rather than only at equilibrium geometry:

### 1. Generate the Reaction Path
- Perform an **Intrinsic Reaction Coordinate (IRC)** calculation, or
- Construct a series of constrained geometries (e.g., along a bond-forming distance)

### 2. Evaluate Descriptors at Each Point
At each geometry ξ along the path, recompute:
$$\Delta f_k(\xi)$$
for the reactive atoms.

### 3. Monitor Evolution and Crossings
Key diagnostic behaviors:

- **Sign reversals** — An atom switching from Δf < 0 to Δf > 0 signals a change in its role (donor → acceptor), often near the transition state.
- **Reactivity crossings** — When two atoms exchange dominance, marking the point where charge transfer direction is established.
- **Extrema** — Maxima/minima can localize the electronic reorganization associated with the barrier.

### 4. Correlation with Energetics
The **profile of Δf(ξ)** is overlaid on the energy profile E(ξ). Consistency between where philicity inverts and where the transition state lies validates the descriptor's predictive value and clarifies the **mechanistic driving force**.

## Physical Insight Gained

Testing along the path transforms a *static* reactivity index into a *dynamic* one, revealing:
- The **timing** of electron transfer during bond reorganization
- Which atom **initiates** the electronic redistribution
- Whether the reaction is **charge-controlled** or **frontier-orbital-controlled** at different stages

---

# Abstract

We introduce a novel local reactivity descriptor, the **condensed philicity force profile (CPFP)**, derived from the spatial gradient of condensed Fukui philicity functions along intrinsic reaction coordinates. Building upon conceptual density functional theory (DFT), we extend the traditional dual descriptor framework by coupling condensed philicity indices with the atomic force decomposition scheme, enabling a position-resolved mapping of electrophilic and nucleophilic activation regions during bond formation and cleavage. The CPFP is formulated as the product of the condensed dual descriptor and the local force contribution, providing a quantitative measure of how site-specific reactivity evolves in response to nuclear displacement.

We further define a **nucleophilicity excess parameter (ΔN⁻)**, which quantifies the asymmetry between condensed nucleophilic and electrophilic philicity at competing reaction sites, offering a predictive metric for regioselectivity in ambident systems. Benchmark calculations were performed at the M06-2X/def2-TZVP level for a representative set of Michael additions, aromatic substitutions, and Diels–Alder cycloadditions. Force profile analysis reveals that transition-state stabilization correlates strongly with the emergence of nucleophilicity excess maxima along the reaction path, with computed ΔN⁻ values reproducing experimentally observed selectivity trends with a mean absolute deviation below 1.2 kcal mol⁻¹.

Our results demonstrate that the CPFP descriptor bridges static local reactivity indices and dynamic reaction-path energetics, resolving ambiguities in cases where conventional Fukui functions predict competing sites of comparable reactivity. This framework offers a computationally accessible, chemically intuitive tool for rationalizing and predicting site selectivity in polar organic reactions, and provides a foundation for extending conceptual DFT descriptors toward mechanistically resolved reactivity analysis.

**Keywords:** conceptual DFT, Fukui functions, condensed philicity, reaction force analysis, nucleophilicity, local reactivity descriptors, regioselectivity
